title: jasonratcliffe.dev: cloud security resume site
goal: Give hiring managers, recruiters and contacts a fast, secure resume site on jasonratcliffe.dev that shows Jason's depth in cloud security through how it is built as much as through what it says.
success: A first-time visitor reaches the full resume, the PDF download and the LinkedIn link within one click from the landing view, and the live site scores A+ on Mozilla Observatory, A on securityheaders.com, and 90+ in every Lighthouse category on mobile.
users: Prospective hiring managers, recruiters and networking contacts who know Jason works in security but not his title or depth; they arrive from LinkedIn, email or a shared link, on a laptop or phone, and may not be terminal users.

must_have.item: Classic resume page with sections Summary, Experience, Certifications, Projects, Skills, Contact, built from the 2025 .docx, with links to LinkedIn, the 3 external AWS posts/talk
must_have.accept: Open https://jasonratcliffe.dev: all six sections are present, every role, date, cert and award from the .docx appears, and nav links jump to each section. LinkedIn opens linkedin.com/in/jasonratcliffe; the 3 AWS blog/AWS TV links from the .docx each open the right page.

must_have.item: View and download a redacted PDF resume generated from the same content
must_have.accept: Click 'Download resume': a PDF opens/downloads; searching it finds no phone number, no street/ZIP address, and no email address, but does show San Antonio, TX and the LinkedIn URL.

must_have.item: Optional terminal overlay (option b): opened by a visible button or the backtick key, closed with Esc
must_have.accept: Press ` or click the terminal button: a terminal opens with focus in the prompt. Type help: a command list prints. whoami, experience, certs, skills, projects, blog, contact, resume, threat-model, arch, clear all produce output; an unknown command prints a hint; Up arrow recalls history; Esc closes it and the page is unchanged.

must_have.item: Architecture page showing how the site is hosted and secured, with generic labels only
must_have.accept: Open /architecture: a diagram shows DNS, CDN, certificate, private origin bucket, security headers, contact API, function, mail service, IaC state and CI/CD with a one-line control note on each; the page source contains no 12-digit account ID, no ARN, no real bucket, distribution or function name.

must_have.item: Threat-model view of Jason's career, mapping STRIDE categories to real work from the resume
must_have.accept: Open /threat-model: six STRIDE categories each list at least one mitigation drawn from the .docx (e.g. SSH key lifecycle, SCP guardrails, data perimeter, PAM); every claim can be traced to a resume line.

must_have.item: Contact form backed by a serverless API (API Gateway, Lambda, SES) that delivers to Jason's inbox from noreply@jasonratcliffe.dev, with the destination address never in the page, repo or Terraform state outputs
must_have.accept: Submit the form with a name, a reply-to and a message: a success message shows and the email arrives in Jason's inbox from noreply@jasonratcliffe.dev. Filling the hidden honeypot field results in no email. Sending 20 requests in a minute triggers throttling (HTTP 429). grep the built site and repo for '@gmail' finds nothing.

must_have.item: On-site blog built from Markdown files in the repo, with an index and per-post pages
must_have.accept: Add a .md file under the blog folder and rebuild: it appears on /blog with title and date and opens at its own URL; the site launches with one post on how this site is built.

must_have.item: ASCII cloud-security animation in the hero that respects reduced motion
must_have.accept: Load the home page: an ASCII animation plays without blocking scroll or text; with the OS 'reduce motion' setting on, a still frame shows instead.

must_have.item: Terraform for all AWS infrastructure: private S3 origin behind CloudFront with OAC, ACM cert, Route 53 hosted zone, security headers policy, SES domain identity (DKIM/SPF/DMARC), contact API; state in a separate encrypted, versioned S3 state bucket with locking
must_have.accept: From a clean checkout, terraform init and plan in the bootstrap module, then in the main module, run without errors; the origin bucket blocks all public access and direct S3 URLs return 403; the state bucket has versioning, encryption and public access block on.

must_have.item: Strong HTTP security posture on the live site
must_have.accept: curl -I https://jasonratcliffe.dev shows Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy without unsafe-inline scripts, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy; http:// redirects to https://; www redirects to the bare domain.

must_have.item: Responsive, accessible layout in a dark, modern cloud-security theme
must_have.accept: At 375px wide nothing scrolls sideways and every section is readable; keyboard Tab reaches every link, the terminal button and the form; Lighthouse accessibility is 90+.

must_have.item: Detailed step-by-step guide for deploying with GitHub Actions (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md): one-time bootstrap, DNS cutover, GitHub OIDC roles, secrets/variables, PR plan workflow, main-branch apply and deploy, verification and rollback
must_have.accept: Following docs/DEPLOYMENT.md top to bottom from a fresh AWS account and empty GitHub repo, every step names the exact command or click, what you should see, and how to fix the common failure; no step requires long-lived AWS access keys in GitHub.

nice_to_have: Self-check widget that shows visitors which response headers the site sends
Terminal easter eggs (e.g. sudo, nmap, cat /etc/shadow with a joke response)
Print stylesheet for the resume page
out_of_scope: Publishing personal contact details (they are a reject_if line)
A CMS or admin login for the blog
A hosted inbox such as Workspace or Fastmail
A paid web application firewall subscription
Transferring the domain registration away from Squarespace
constraints: Static site hosted from S3 via CloudFront; the only server-side piece is the contact Lambda
Terraform only for infrastructure, state in its own S3 bucket
No real resource names, ARNs or AWS account IDs in public site content; account-specific values live in a git-ignored tfvars file
DNS delegated from Squarespace to Route 53 by pasting four nameservers (one manual step for Jason)
Running cost target under $2/month at low traffic

assumptions.text: Deploys run from GitHub Actions using AWS OIDC: PRs get a read-only plan role, pushes to main get an apply role gated by a 'production' environment; a 'make deploy' fallback exists for the laptop.
Site is built with Astro (static output, Markdown blog, no client framework); the terminal and animation are small vanilla TypeScript modules.
Content comes from the .docx only; LinkedIn is linked, not scraped, because it requires login.
Employer name (USAA), awards and the public AWS blog posts may be shown as written in the resume.
Success targets (one-click resume, Observatory A+, securityheaders A, Lighthouse 90+) stand in for the success question you skipped.
Look is dark, terminal-adjacent: near-black background, one cyan/teal accent, monospace for code and headings, sans-serif for body text.
SES stays in sandbox mode, which works because it only ever sends to Jason's own verified address.
Infrastructure goes in us-east-1 (required for the CloudFront certificate; keeps everything in one region).
Resume text is lightly tightened for the web (shorter bullets on the page), and the full wording is kept in the PDF.
You are the only approver, and there is no hard deadline.

reject_if: Phone, home address or any email address appears on the site, in the PDF, or in the public repo
A real AWS account ID, ARN or resource name appears in site content
A recruiter has to use the terminal to find the resume
Any resume fact on the site differs from the .docx (title, dates, certs, awards, numbers)
The origin S3 bucket is publicly readable
open_risks: DNS cutover depends on Jason updating nameservers in Squarespace; propagation can take up to 48 hours and will break any existing Squarespace site on the domain
SES domain verification and DKIM need the Route 53 zone to be live first, so the contact form only works after DNS propagates
The public repo must never contain the tfvars file with the account ID and destination email; a pre-commit secret/PII scan guards it
